To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the immune system can recognize platelet antigens, and that this recognition can cause platelet destruction.
the immune response to the platelet antigens can lead to platelet destruction and thrombocytosis.
platelets are not merely the passive victims of immune responses but are actively involved in the immune responses that target them.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the immune system's response to platelet antigens, the biological mechanisms that lead to the destruction of platelets in vivo and how this knowledge can be used to reduce the impact of these adverse conditions.
the biology of platelet antigens, their immune recognition, the effector mechanisms that cause thrombocytocytopenia and the potential for platelets to influence their own destruction.
understanding the biological basis of the immune response against platelet antigens.

platelets are both the ‘prey and predator’ in this scenario.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
platelets have the ability to both initiate and suppress an immune response.
platelets are both prey and predators of the immune system.
platelets can be seen to have a dual role in the immune response: they are a target of immune destruction and they also play a role as an immune effector mechanism.
The main takeaway from our work is that
platelets are not simply the ‘passengers’ in blood, but rather they play a role in the regulation of the immune system.
